Apple officially announced its "Apple Upgrade" leasing program today, and it works exactly as the outside world expected. Although the plan allows consumers to acquire products at a lower monthly fee, it may trap users in an endless cycle of leasing.

The reason is that, unlike the "iPhone Upgrade Program" which it partially replaces, users will not directly own the device after the lease period ends……

As Apple product prices continue to rise, the ability to make products more accessible through instalments does hold a certain appeal. Judging solely by the monthly payment amount, the "Apple Upgrade" plan does achieve this.

For example, users can lease a MacBook Pro equipped with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage for as little as US$38.99 per month. This approach makes Apple products more affordable for more consumers, which is undoubtedly a good thing.

The hidden concerns of the "Apple Upgrade" plan

However, the problem is exactly as I predicted last week: users will use this plan just like leasing a car. Although you can choose to pay the residual value at the end of the lease period to take ownership of the car, almost nobody does this. Most car lessees return the car and then lease a new one, repeating the same cycle endlessly.

The same situation could occur with the "Apple Upgrade" plan. To fully own the device, users must pay a lump sum equal to the difference between the total rent and the original price of the product.

Let us use the MacBook Pro mentioned earlier as an example (amounts rounded to the nearest dollar):

36-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$38.99
  • Total expenditure over the entire lease period: US$1,403
  • Residual value required to buy out the device: US$585

24-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$53.99
  • Total expenditure over the entire lease period: US$1,295
  • Residual value required to buy out the device: US$703

For people who cannot afford the full purchase price of the device from the outset, finding a sum of money like this at short notice is no easy task. Unless they save a set amount throughout the lease period, there is a high chance they will struggle to make the payment. If that is the case, the most likely outcome is that they will start a new lease cycle all over again.

If you can afford it, the more advanced approach is……

If you can afford a higher monthly outlay, the smarter approach is to modify the plan yourself into something resembling the old IUP model.

On one hand, you pay Apple the monthly rent; on the other, you simultaneously deposit a sum of money into a savings account each month, in preparation for paying the residual value at the end of the lease period. Taking that 36-month MBP lease as an example, the calculation works out as follows:

  • Monthly rent: US$38.99
  • Monthly deposit into savings account: US$16.26
  • Total monthly expenditure: US$55.25
  • Total amount paid to Apple: US$1,403
  • Total amount in savings account (for paying the residual value): US$585.36 (plus any interest earned)

The most upvoted comment was posted by Ryan Lounsbury

I would very likely use this leasing plan to buy my iPhone. I upgrade my phone every 12 to 24 months. So, assuming no interest at all, I could simply keep using the latest handset, return the old one at the end of the contract for a new one, and never have to pay for the full cost of the phone in one go. For someone with my upgrading habits, this approach makes perfect sense.

However, Apple has slipped a "poison pill" into the Upgrade/Lease plan, requiring users to select and activate service with a designated carrier. I have been with Mint Mobile for many years, so this means I am unable to use this leasing plan, and I would even have to pay a fee because I did not activate it through one of their "approved" carriers. It is really annoying.

After that, you can use the money in your savings account to pay that US$585 residual value, and the device will officially be yours, free and clear.

Of course, if you really want to upgrade to a new device, you are absolutely free to sell the one you currently own and start a new lease. The price you fetch on the second-hand market will most likely be enough to cover the residual value of the new device, and you can deposit that money straight into your savings account, leaving your monthly outlay as just the rent.

How are you planning to handle your future Apple product expenses? Feel free to share in the comments section.
